# Force-Based Haptic Feedback and Menu Navigation Method

## Overview

The described method provides a system for interpreting force-based user input and translating it into coordinated haptic feedback and menu navigation. By combining force sensing, temporal analysis, and proportional haptic response, the method enables intuitive interaction between a user and a menu-driven interface.

## Force Signal Reception and Magnitude Determination

The method begins when it receives a force signal generated by a force sensor. This force sensor detects physical input applied by a user—such as a press or sustained pressure—and transmits a corresponding signal to the system. Upon receiving this signal, the method processes it to determine the force magnitude associated with the input, thereby quantifying the amount of pressure the user is applying.

## Threshold Comparison and Duration Measurement

Once the force magnitude has been established, the system compares it against an initial threshold value. This comparison determines whether the applied force exceeds a predefined minimum required to register a valid input, helping to distinguish intentional interactions from incidental contact. When the force magnitude surpasses the initial threshold, the system begins measuring the duration for which the magnitude remains above that threshold. This temporal measurement ensures that only sustained inputs—rather than momentary or accidental touches—are treated as deliberate commands.

## Haptic Feedback Generation

If the measured elapsed time exceeds a defined minimum elapsed time, the method proceeds to generate a haptic feedback control signal. This signal is used to drive a haptic actuator, which produces a tactile response perceptible to the user. By requiring both a sufficient force magnitude and a minimum duration, the system confirms the user's intent before initiating feedback.

## Proportional Pressure Wave Propagation

Upon receiving the haptic feedback control signal, the haptic actuator propagates multiple pressure waves. Notably, these pressure waves are propagated at a propagation frequency that is directly proportional to the force magnitude. As a result, the intensity or rhythm of the tactile feedback varies in accordance with how firmly the user presses—greater applied force produces a higher propagation frequency, while lighter force produces a lower one. This proportional relationship allows the user to perceive, through touch alone, the degree of force they are applying.

## Coordinated Menu Scrolling

In parallel with the haptic response, the method generates a scroll control signal. This signal causes a menu system to scroll through its available options at a scroll frequency that is associated with the propagation frequency of the pressure waves. Because both the haptic feedback and the menu scrolling are linked to the force magnitude, the user experiences a unified and responsive interface: increasing the applied force accelerates both the tactile feedback and the rate at which menu options advance. This coordination provides the user with precise, force-modulated control over navigation while receiving continuous tactile confirmation of their input.

## Summary

Taken together, these steps define a cohesive method in which user-applied force is sensed, validated through threshold and duration checks, and then translated into synchronized haptic feedback and menu navigation. The proportional relationship between force magnitude, pressure wave propagation, and scroll frequency creates an intuitive and tactile means of interacting with a menu system.

# Force-Sensitive Haptic Feedback for Intuitive Menu Navigation

## Overview

This document describes a method and system for controlling haptic feedback in response to user-applied force, enabling intuitive navigation through menu options. The approach combines force sensing, temporal validation, and coordinated haptic and visual feedback to create a responsive and natural user experience.

## Receiving and Evaluating the Force Sensor Signal

The method begins when the system receives a signal from a force sensor. This sensor is configured to detect the magnitude of force applied by a user—for example, when the user presses against a surface, button, or touch-sensitive region of a device. The incoming signal represents a continuous or sampled measurement of the applied pressure.

Once received, the magnitude of the force sensor signal is compared against an **initial threshold**. This threshold serves as a gatekeeping value: only forces that exceed this baseline level are considered intentional inputs worthy of triggering a system response. By establishing this initial threshold, the system effectively filters out incidental or accidental contact, reducing the likelihood of unintended activations.

## Temporal Validation Through Minimum Duration

In addition to satisfying the force magnitude requirement, the system measures the **elapsed time** during which the applied force is sustained. This measured duration is compared against a predefined **minimum duration** threshold. The system will only proceed to trigger a response if the applied force both exceeds the initial magnitude threshold *and* persists for longer than this minimum duration.

This dual-condition approach ensures that only deliberate, sustained inputs activate the feedback mechanism. A brief tap or momentary spike in force—even one that momentarily exceeds the magnitude threshold—will not trigger the response unless the user maintains the pressure for the required period of time. This provides an added layer of intentionality to the interaction.

## Generating the Haptic and Navigational Response

When both conditions are satisfied—sufficient force magnitude sustained beyond the minimum duration—the system initiates a coordinated response consisting of two simultaneous actions:

### 1. Haptic Feedback via Pressure Waves

The system generates haptic feedback in the form of **pressure waves** delivered to the user. Critically, these pressure waves are produced at a **propagation frequency that is proportional to the magnitude of the applied force**. This means that as the user presses harder, the propagation frequency of the haptic pulses increases correspondingly, while a lighter touch produces feedback at a lower frequency. This proportional relationship gives the user immediate, tactile awareness of how much force they are applying, creating a closed feedback loop between input and sensation.

### 2. Scrolling Through Menu Options

Simultaneously with the haptic feedback, the system scrolls through the available **menu options** at a **scroll frequency** that corresponds to the applied force. Just as with the haptic feedback, a greater applied force results in faster scrolling, while a lighter force produces slower, more controlled scrolling. This allows the user to modulate their navigation speed simply by varying the pressure they apply.

## Benefits and Advantages

By linking both the haptic propagation frequency and the menu scroll frequency to the magnitude of the applied force, the system delivers a unified, force-sensitive interaction model. The user can intuitively control the pace of menu navigation while receiving continuous tactile confirmation of their input intensity. Faster scrolling naturally coincides with more rapid haptic pulses, reinforcing the user's sense of control.

The combination of the initial force threshold and the minimum duration requirement ensures that navigation is only triggered by intentional inputs, while the proportional feedback mechanisms make the experience feel natural and responsive. Together, these features enable **force-sensitive, intuitive menu navigation** that is both precise and satisfying to use.

# Implementations: Turning Ideas into Reality

## What Are Implementations?

An implementation refers to the process of putting a plan, design, decision, or concept into practical effect. It is the critical bridge between abstract ideas and tangible outcomes. Whether in software development, business strategy, public policy, or engineering, implementations transform theoretical frameworks into working systems that produce real-world results.

## The Importance of Effective Implementation

A brilliant idea holds little value if it cannot be successfully executed. History is filled with promising strategies and innovative concepts that failed not because they were flawed in principle, but because their implementations were poorly managed. Effective implementation determines whether goals are met, resources are used efficiently, and stakeholders remain satisfied.

## Common Types of Implementations

**Software Implementations**
In technology, an implementation often refers to the actual code that realizes a specification or algorithm. Different programming languages may offer distinct implementations of the same concept, each with unique performance characteristics and trade-offs.

**Business and Organizational Implementations**
Companies implement new processes, systems, and policies to improve productivity, adapt to market changes, or comply with regulations. These implementations require careful change management and employee buy-in.

**Policy Implementations**
Governments and institutions implement laws, programs, and initiatives designed to serve public interests. Successful policy implementation depends on adequate funding, clear communication, and effective enforcement.

## Key Factors for Successful Implementation

1. **Clear Planning** – Well-defined objectives and detailed roadmaps guide the process.
2. **Resource Allocation** – Sufficient time, budget, and personnel must be dedicated.
3. **Communication** – Stakeholders should understand goals, roles, and expectations.
4. **Monitoring and Evaluation** – Continuous assessment helps identify problems early.
5. **Flexibility** – The ability to adapt when circumstances change is essential.

## Common Challenges

Implementations frequently encounter obstacles such as resistance to change, inadequate resources, unrealistic timelines, and unforeseen technical difficulties. Overcoming these challenges requires strong leadership, thorough preparation, and a willingness to learn from setbacks.

## Conclusion

Implementations are the vital phase where vision meets execution. No matter how sophisticated a plan may be, its ultimate success rests on how well it is carried out. By prioritizing careful planning, clear communication, and adaptive management, organizations and individuals can ensure that their implementations deliver meaningful and lasting results.

# Patent Claim Summary: Haptic Feedback Control Method Based on Force Sensor Input

## Abstract Summary

A method for controlling haptic feedback in an electronic device, wherein force sensor input is used to simultaneously modulate tactile feedback characteristics and control menu scrolling operations.

---

## Independent Claim (Example)

**1.** A method for controlling haptic feedback in an electronic device, the method comprising:

- **detecting**, via at least one force sensor, an applied force corresponding to a user input;

- **determining** a magnitude of the applied force relative to one or more predetermined force thresholds;

- **generating** a haptic feedback signal having at least one characteristic that varies based on the determined magnitude of the applied force;

- **controlling** a scrolling operation of a menu displayed on a display of the electronic device, wherein a scrolling parameter is adjusted in correspondence with the determined magnitude of the applied force; and

- **synchronizing** the haptic feedback signal with the scrolling operation such that tactile feedback is provided as the menu advances through discrete selectable items.

---

## Dependent Claims (Examples)

**2.** The method of claim 1, wherein the scrolling parameter comprises a scrolling speed that increases proportionally with the applied force.

**3.** The method of claim 1, wherein the at least one characteristic of the haptic feedback signal comprises amplitude, frequency, or duration.

**4.** The method of claim 1, wherein a distinct haptic pulse is generated as each menu item boundary is traversed.

**5.** The method of claim 1, further comprising selecting a menu item when the applied force exceeds a selection threshold greater than a scrolling threshold.

---

## Key Elements Summary

| Element | Function |
|---------|----------|
| **Force Sensor** | Detects magnitude of user-applied pressure |
| **Threshold Comparison** | Distinguishes between input intensity levels |
| **Haptic Actuator** | Delivers variable tactile feedback |
| **Menu Controller** | Adjusts scroll speed/position based on force |
| **Synchronization Logic** | Coordinates haptic response with scroll events |

---

*Note: This is a template summary for illustrative purposes. Actual patent claims should be drafted or reviewed by a registered patent attorney to ensure proper scope, novelty, and compliance with applicable patent laws.*

# SUMMARY

The following summary is provided to introduce a selection of concepts in a simplified form that are further described below in the Detailed Description. This summary is not intended to identify key features or essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor is it intended to be used to limit the scope of the claimed subject matter.

Embodiments described herein relate to systems, methods, and computer-readable media for generating haptic feedback and controlling scroll operations based on a combination of force magnitude and elapsed time associated with a user input.

In one aspect, a method is disclosed comprising receiving, via a force-sensing input surface, an input signal indicative of a force applied to the input surface. A force magnitude associated with the input signal is determined, and the force magnitude is compared against one or more force thresholds. Concurrently, an elapsed time during which the applied force satisfies at least one of the one or more force thresholds is measured. In response to determining that the force magnitude satisfies a first force threshold and that the elapsed time satisfies a first time threshold, a haptic feedback signal is generated to cause a haptic output device to produce a tactile response. In response to determining that the force magnitude and the elapsed time satisfy a second set of criteria, a scroll control signal is generated to initiate, modify, or terminate a scroll operation on a display.

In some embodiments, a rate of the scroll operation is dynamically adjusted as a function of at least one of the force magnitude and the elapsed time. For example, an increasing force magnitude may proportionally increase a scroll velocity, while a sustained force over an increasing elapsed time may accelerate the scroll operation. In further embodiments, distinct haptic feedback patterns are generated to indicate a transition between force thresholds, thereby providing the user with tactile confirmation that a scroll operation has been initiated, that a scroll rate has changed, or that a boundary of scrollable content has been reached.

In another aspect, a system is disclosed comprising a force-sensing input surface, a haptic output device, a display, one or more processors, and memory storing instructions that, when executed by the one or more processors, cause the system to perform operations in accordance with the methods described herein. The coordinated use of both force magnitude and elapsed time as triggering conditions enables the system to distinguish between transient inputs, deliberate sustained inputs, and varying degrees of user intent, thereby reducing inadvertent activations and providing an intuitive, responsive user experience.

The features, functions, and advantages discussed herein may be achieved independently in various embodiments or may be combined in yet other embodiments, further details of which may be seen with reference to the following description and drawings.

measuring, via a force sensor, an applied force at an input surface;

comparing, via a processor, the measured applied force to a predetermined force threshold;

in response to the measured applied force satisfying the predetermined force threshold, scrolling through a plurality of menu options presented on a display; and

generating, via a haptic actuator, one or more pressure waves having a magnitude proportional to the measured applied force during the scrolling through the plurality of menu options.

# Haptic Actuator Control System with Force-Magnitude-Dependent Propagation Frequency

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

[0001] The present invention relates generally to haptic feedback systems, and more particularly to methods and apparatus for controlling one or more haptic actuators wherein a propagation frequency of a haptic waveform is modulated as a function of an applied force magnitude, and further wherein said propagation frequency is coordinated with a scroll frequency associated with a user interface element.

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

[0002] Conventional haptic feedback systems typically produce a fixed vibratory response upon detection of a user input event. Such systems fail to convey nuanced information regarding the magnitude of force applied by a user, resulting in a haptic experience that is disconnected from the physical characteristics of the interaction.

[0003] Moreover, in user interfaces incorporating scrollable elements, existing haptic implementations produce feedback that is temporally decoupled from the rate at which interface elements traverse a display region. There exists a need for a haptic control system in which the character of tactile feedback is dynamically tied to both applied force and interface motion.

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

[0004] In accordance with one aspect of the invention, a haptic control system is provided comprising: (a) at least one force sensor configured to generate a force signal representative of a force magnitude applied to an input surface; (b) at least one haptic actuator; and (c) a controller configured to generate a drive signal for the haptic actuator, wherein a propagation frequency of the drive signal is determined as a function of the force magnitude.

[0005] In accordance with a further aspect, the propagation frequency is additionally coordinated with a menu scroll frequency, such that a substantially deterministic relationship is maintained between the rate of tactile propagation events and the rate at which discrete menu items traverse a reference position.

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION

### System Architecture

[0006] Referring to the implementation, the system comprises a force-sensitive input surface operatively coupled to one or more force sensors. Suitable force sensors include, without limitation, capacitive strain sensors, piezoresistive elements, piezoelectric transducers, or displacement-based sensors. The force sensor produces a force signal *F(t)* representing an instantaneous force magnitude.

[0007] The haptic actuator may comprise a linear resonant actuator (LRA), an eccentric rotating mass (ERM) actuator, a piezoelectric actuator, or an electroactive polymer actuator. In a preferred embodiment, an LRA is employed owing to its favorable transient response characteristics.

### Force-Dependent Propagation Frequency

[0008] The controller computes a propagation frequency *f_p* according to a mapping function:

> *f_p* = **Φ**(*F*)

wherein **Φ** is a monotonic function of the force magnitude *F*. In one embodiment, the mapping is substantially linear:

> *f_p* = *f_0* + *k* · (*F* − *F_th*)

where *f_0* denotes a baseline propagation frequency, *k* denotes a proportionality constant, and *F_th* denotes a threshold force below which no propagation event is generated.

[0009] In an alternative embodiment, the mapping function **Φ** is non-linear, for example logarithmic or piecewise-linear, so as to approximate human tactile perception which follows an approximately logarithmic response to stimulus intensity (consistent with the Weber-Fechner relationship).

[0010] As used herein, the term "propagation frequency" refers to the repetition rate at which discrete haptic events—each comprising a transient actuator displacement or "tactile pulse"—are propagated to the user. Thus, as the applied force increases, the temporal density of tactile pulses increases, producing a perceptually intensifying feedback sensation.

### Relationship to Menu Scroll Frequency

[0011] In embodiments incorporating a scrollable user interface, a menu scroll frequency *f_s* is defined as the rate at which discrete menu items pass a designated reference position (for example, a selection indicator or display centerline). The scroll frequency is itself a function of a scroll velocity *v_s* and an inter-item spacing *d*:

> *f_s* = *v_s* / *d*

[0012] The controller establishes a coordination relationship between the propagation frequency *f_p* and the menu scroll frequency *f_s*. In a first embodiment, the propagation frequency is locked to the scroll frequency according to an integer or rational multiplier *N*:

> *f_p* = *N* · *f_s*

such that each discrete menu item traversal is accompanied by *N* tactile pulses. Where *N* = 1, a single tactile detent is generated per menu item.

[0013] In a second embodiment, the force magnitude modulates the multiplier *N* itself, such that:

> *N* = **Ψ**(*F*)

whereby a user applying a greater force experiences a proportionally greater density of tactile events per menu item, enriching the tactile texture during forceful interactions while maintaining coarse detent feedback during light interactions.

[0014] In a third embodiment, the scroll velocity *v_s* is itself derived from the force magnitude, for example in a force-controlled or pressure-based scrolling paradigm, whereby increased force induces increased scroll velocity. In such an embodiment, the propagation frequency and the scroll frequency co-vary as coupled functions of the common force input, maintaining perceptual coherence between the visual scrolling motion and the tactile feedback.

### Synchronization and Phase Control

[0015] The controller may further include a phase-locking subsystem configured to align individual tactile pulses with the arrival of each menu item at the reference position. Phase alignment reduces perceptual dissonance between visual and tactile modalities. The phase relationship may be expressed as a phase offset *θ* applied to the drive signal to compensate for actuator rise-time latency.

### Example Method of Operation

[0016] In operation, the method comprises the steps of:

- (a) receiving, from the force sensor, a force signal indicative of an applied force magnitude;
- (b) computing a propagation frequency as a function of the force magnitude;
- (c) determining a menu scroll frequency associated with a scrollable interface element;
- (d) coordinating the propagation frequency with the menu scroll frequency according to a predetermined relationship;
- (e) generating a haptic drive signal having the coordinated propagation frequency; and
- (f) applying the drive signal to the haptic actuator to produce a sequence of tactile pulses perceptible to the user.

## CLAIMS

What is claimed is:

**1.** A haptic feedback system comprising: a force sensor configured to produce a force signal representative of an applied force magnitude; a haptic actuator; and a controller configured to generate a drive signal for said haptic actuator, wherein a propagation frequency of said drive signal is determined as a monotonic function of said force magnitude.

**2.** The system of claim 1, wherein said controller coordinates said propagation frequency with a menu scroll frequency associated with a scrollable user interface element.

**3.** The system of claim 2, wherein said propagation frequency is an integer or rational multiple of said menu scroll frequency.

**4.** The system of claim 2, wherein a multiplier relating said propagation frequency to said menu scroll frequency is itself a function of said force magnitude.

**5.** The system of claim 1, wherein said monotonic function is one of a linear, logarithmic, or piecewise-linear function of said force magnitude.

**6.** The system of claim 2, further comprising a phase-locking subsystem configured to align individual tactile pulses with arrival of respective menu items at a reference position.

**7.** A method of controlling a haptic actuator, comprising: receiving a force signal indicative of an applied force magnitude; computing a propagation frequency as a function of said force magnitude; determining a menu scroll frequency; coordinating said propagation frequency with said menu scroll frequency; and driving said haptic actuator with a drive signal having said coordinated propagation frequency.

---

*Note: This document is a stylistic illustration written in the format and register of a utility patent specification. It does not constitute legal advice, a filed application, or a representation of patentability, and should be reviewed by a qualified patent professional before any actual use.*
